transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I'm here because... I just can't stop focusing on how I look. Mostly my hairline, and just the way my face looks. I work as a host at a restaurant, and under those lights, I just look really old and... strange. It takes up all my thoughts. My coworkers keep telling me they don't see what I'm talking about, but I know what I see, and I just can't stop thinking about it.
When you're thinking about your appearance, do you find yourself doing anything repetitive with your hair or skin, like pulling out hairs, picking at your skin, or anything like that?

No, I don't really pick at my skin or pull my hair out. But I do repeat other things. Like, right before a shift, I just keep checking the bathroom mirror. I'll take pictures on my phone from all these different angles to see how bad it looks, and I spend a lot of time just combing my hair forward, trying to hide it. 

I also just keep replaying in my head exactly how the guests might see me when they walk in. I do it over and over until I'm either late for work, or I just get too worked up to even go out to the front stand.

When you look in the mirror and see these problems with your hairline and face, do you think most people would notice these same flaws if they looked at you, or do you think this might be something that's mostly noticeable to you?

I honestly don't know for sure. Like I said earlier, my coworkers tell me they don't see what I'm talking about. But... when I look in the mirror, it's just so obvious to me. 

It feels like every customer walking into the restaurant must be staring right at my hairline and how old my face looks. So, I guess I'm not entirely sure if strangers actually notice it as much as I do, or if it's mostly just me. I just know what I see, and it's hard not to feel like everyone else must be seeing it too.

When you really think about it logically, do you believe that your hairline and face are actually as noticeable and problematic as your mind tells you they are, or do you suspect that your concern might be out of proportion to how others actually perceive you?

I'm not really sure how to answer that. I try to think about it logically, but... it's hard. I hear what my coworkers say, so maybe part of me wonders if I'm making it a bigger deal than it is. 

But then I look in the mirror, and it's just right there. It feels so real to me. So I really don't know if my concern is out of proportion or not. I just know how bad it looks to me, and it's really hard to get past that, no matter how much I try to rationalize it.

When you think about what your coworkers are telling you—that they don't see these flaws—does any part of you believe they might actually be right, or are you pretty convinced that they're just being nice or not looking closely enough?

I really couldn't tell you. Um... sometimes I think they're just being polite, you know, because we have to work together every day. Or maybe they just aren't looking that closely since the lighting in the restaurant is kind of dim and we're usually rushing around. 

But I can't say for sure. I don't know if they actually mean it when they say I look fine, or if they're just humoring me to get me to stop talking about it. I just really don't know what to believe anymore.

If you were to step back and think about it from a completely neutral perspective, do you think it's possible that your concern about your hairline and face might be more intense than what most other people would feel about similar minor changes to their appearance?

I don't know. I guess if I step back, maybe? But it's hard to be neutral about it. I mean, I hear what you're saying, that maybe I'm reacting more intensely than someone else might. But to me, these don't feel like minor changes. They feel huge. So I can't really say how other people would feel, because I'm just dealing with how I feel, and it's... it's overwhelming. I just don't know.

When your coworkers tell you they don't see these flaws you're describing, does any part of you think there's a real possibility they might actually be telling you the truth, or do you feel fairly certain that what you see in the mirror is definitely real regardless of what they say?

I honestly just don't know. Like I was saying a minute ago, I can't really tell you for sure one way or the other. 

When I look in the mirror, what I see is definitely real to me. It's right there. But then they say they don't see it... so I'm just stuck. I don't know if there's a real possibility they're telling the truth, or if they're just being nice. I just know what I see, and it's hard to ignore that, but I really don't know what to believe beyond that.

If you were to imagine that your coworkers are being completely honest with you and they truly don't see these flaws, how would that change the way you understand what's happening? Would it make you think that maybe your mind is playing tricks on you, or would you still feel certain that the flaws are there?

I... I'm really not sure. If they are being completely honest, and they truly don't see it... I guess that would mean something is off with how I'm seeing myself. But even if I try to imagine that, it's just so hard to wrap my head around. 

Because when I look in the mirror, it's just so obvious to me. It's right there. So even if they're telling the truth, I think I would still feel like the flaws are there. I don't know if I could just turn off what I'm seeing, even if I wanted to believe them. I just don't know how to make sense of it.

If I were to tell you that based on what your coworkers are saying, there's strong evidence that these flaws you're seeing might not actually be as visible or as severe as they appear to you in the mirror, would you be able to consider that as a real possibility, or does what you see in the mirror feel too certain to doubt?

I mean... I hear what you're saying about the evidence. But honestly? What I see in the mirror just feels too certain. 

I can try to tell myself that maybe it's not as bad as I think, but the second I look at my reflection, it all just comes rushing back. It's so severe to me. So... no, I don't think I can really consider it a possibility. What I see is just too real to me, no matter what anyone else says.

When you think about all the times your coworkers have told you they don't see these flaws, and considering how consistently they've said this, do you think there's any chance—even a small one—that your brain might be exaggerating or distorting how you see your reflection, rather than everyone else just being blind to real flaws?

I don't know. I mean, I guess anything is possible, but... no, I don't really think my brain is exaggerating it. When I look in the mirror, I'm not imagining things. I see exactly what's there. It's not a distortion, it's just my face. I hear them when they say they don't see it, but I just don't understand how they can't. It's right there in front of me every single day.

When you really think hard about it, is there any possibility—even a small one—that what you're seeing in the mirror might be your brain's interpretation of your appearance rather than an objective reality that everyone else is simply missing?

I just... I don't see how that could be. I mean, I'm looking right at it. It's not an interpretation, it's just my reflection. I know you're trying to help me see it differently, but I can't just pretend I don't see what's right there in front of me. I don't think my brain is making it up. It's just... it's just what I look like.

Looking back at everything we've discussed, if I told you that based on all the evidence from your coworkers and the objective facts, the most likely explanation is that your concerns about your appearance are much more severe than what's actually there, would you be able to accept that as possibly true, or does it feel impossible to believe that?

I know we've gone over this, and I hear what you're saying about the evidence and my coworkers. But... it really does just feel impossible to believe. 

I just can't accept it as being true. I mean, I look at myself every single day, and the flaws are right there. It's not something I can just talk myself out of or pretend isn't happening. So, no... I really can't see it as just being in my head. What I see is what's there.

When you hear your coworkers say they don't see these flaws, and you think about how consistently they've all said the same thing, does any part of you wonder if maybe your eyes or your brain might be showing you something that isn't actually as bad as it seems—even if you can't quite believe it?

Look, I know you keep asking me this in different ways. But... no, I really don't wonder that. I don't think my eyes are tricking me. 

When the people at the restaurant say they don't see it... I just figure they're being nice, or maybe they just aren't looking that closely at me. My vision is fine. I'm looking right at the mirror, and it really is exactly as bad as I'm telling you. I don't have any doubts about what I'm seeing.

You've mentioned that when you look in the mirror, the flaws feel completely real and obvious to you. But given that every single coworker has told you they don't see these problems, do you think it's at least possible that your brain might be focusing on or magnifying small details that most people wouldn't notice the same way?

I... I really don't think so. I know you're trying to find a reason why they don't see it, but I'm not magnifying anything. It's not a small detail that I'm just focusing too much on. It's right there. It's obvious. I don't know why they don't see it, or why they say they don't, but I know what I'm looking at. My brain isn't making it worse than it is.

If I were to show you a photo of yourself that your coworkers took, would you be able to look at it objectively and consider that maybe what you see in the mirror doesn't match what's actually in the photo?

I don't think a photo would change anything. If you showed me a picture my coworkers took, I would just see exactly what I see in the mirror. 

I mean... cameras just capture what's actually there. So, no, I wouldn't be able to look at it and say it doesn't match. It would match, because the flaws are real. I'm not sure how else to explain it to you, but a picture isn't going to suddenly make me see something different.
